newsitem.title: USA: SEC weighs in on Moody's muni rating modifiers.
newsitem.headline: SEC weighs in on Moody's muni rating modifiers.

text.p: The SEC said that muni bond issuers do not have to notify national information repositories when Moody's Investors Service, a unit of Dun & Bradstreet Corp., initially adds a "modifier," such as numbers two or three, to their ratings.

That is the case, the Securities and Exchange Commission added, as long as the modification is done as part of an "overall refinement" of Moody's rating system and does not reflect a change in Moody's view of a municipal credit.
Catherine McGuire, SEC's chief counsel for market regulation, offered the interpretation in a one-page response to a query by bond lawyer John McNally, a partner with Hawkins, Delafield & Wood here.
Moody's in January broadened its ratings scale to include new modifiers, the numbers "2" and "3." A rating that was Aa is now either Aa2 or Aa3 under the new program.

McNally wanted to know whether his issuer clients that saw their ratings revised in January have to report the changes to Nationally Recognized Municipal Securities Information Repositories (NRMSIRs).
NRMSIRs were set up under an SEC rule on muni secondary market disclosure that took effect in July 1995.
The amended rule essentially requires bond issuers to contract with dealers to disclose annual financial information and notices of "material" events, including ratings changes.

McGuire said in her letter: "We do not believe the initial assignment by Moody's of a modifier to a rating symbol, done as part of an overall refinement of its rating system, that is not intended to reflect any change in Moody's assessment of the credit supporting an issue of municipal securities, is the type of event for which reporting was intended" under the SEC's 1995 rule.
